turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Morning. I've the observations done. Blood pressure is one hundred and forty-eight over eighty-six, heart rate seventy-two, oxygen saturations ninety-seven percent, and the weight on our scales is eighty-six point five kilograms.
[SEG0002] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Eighty-six point five? Ah no, sure she was seventy-nine kilos at the chemist last month. I was standing beside her.
[SEG0003] person_3 (PATIENT): I don't know, doctor. I don't look at scales. They only annoy me.
[SEG0004] person_4 (DOCTOR): Thanks, Niamh, that's grand. We'll come back to the weight. Sit yourself down. What's been the bother?
[SEG0005] person_3 (PATIENT): It's this knee. On the stairs, mostly. I don't know where to start with it.
[SEG0006] person_4 (DOCTOR): Anywhere you like. Which knee is it, and what does it do?
[SEG0007] person_3 (PATIENT): The right one. Going down the stairs it catches me. Going up is grand. And at night, if I turn over, it aches.
[SEG0008] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): It's three months now. She won't say it, but it has her awake every single night.
[SEG0009] person_3 (PATIENT): Three months? It's not, it's since the summer, six months I'd say, maybe. I don't know the exact day. And it does not have me awake every night, I sleep mostly.
[SEG0010] person_4 (DOCTOR): All right. Six months by you, three by your daughter, and we won't pin the day down. You do get some sleep.
[SEG0011] person_4 (DOCTOR): Does the knee swell at all, or give way, or lock on you?
[SEG0012] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): It swells. I've seen it myself, of an evening, the right one bigger than the left.
[SEG0013] person_3 (PATIENT): I don't know, doctor. I haven't seen it swell. It doesn't give way, and it doesn't lock. It's a deep ache, that's all.
[SEG0014] person_4 (DOCTOR): A deep ache, then. What have you been using for it?
[SEG0015] person_3 (PATIENT): The gel. Diclofenac, from the chemist. I rub it on the right knee morning and night, and it helps a bit.
[SEG0016] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She takes the diclofenac tablets as well, every day. I leave them by the kettle so she won't forget.
[SEG0017] person_3 (PATIENT): I do not take them every day, only sometimes, when the stairs are desperate. A few times in the week, maybe. I don't know how often, I forget.
[SEG0018] person_1 (NURSE): Sorry, I'll just jump in. The box in the bag is diclofenac, fifty milligrams.
[SEG0019] person_3 (PATIENT): Fifty? I thought they were twenty-five, the small ones. I don't know, doctor. Your man in the chemist handed them to me and I didn't ask.
[SEG0020] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The packet at home says fifty milligrams, Mam. You're thinking of an old box.
[SEG0021] person_4 (DOCTOR): We'll not guess the strength, so. Any bother on the skin from the gel?
[SEG0022] person_3 (PATIENT): No. No rash. The gel is grand.
[SEG0023] person_4 (DOCTOR): And the tablets, any stomach trouble? Heartburn, an upset, anything like that?
[SEG0024] person_3 (PATIENT): No. No stomach problems. I'm fine with them.
[SEG0025] person_4 (DOCTOR): Good. How's the appetite, and the energy, apart from the knee?
[SEG0026] person_3 (PATIENT): The appetite is too good, that's half the weight. I'm not tired in myself. The stairs are the knee, not me being wrecked. I don't know how else to put it.
[SEG0027] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She still wants the potatoes every day. Big ones.
[SEG0028] person_4 (DOCTOR): We'll not fight the potatoes just yet. Any other medicines I should know about?
[SEG0029] person_3 (PATIENT): Amlodipine. The blood pressure one. Five milligrams, every morning. I've been on it for years, and I don't miss that one.
[SEG0030] person_4 (DOCTOR): Five milligrams each morning, noted. Anything else at all?
[SEG0031] person_3 (PATIENT): There was a vitamin. I never took it. I don't think there's anything else. I don't know.
[SEG0032] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The vitamin D is in the press, still sealed. And there's paracetamol, but she won't touch it.
[SEG0033] person_3 (PATIENT): I don't take the paracetamol. They do nothing for me.
[SEG0034] person_4 (DOCTOR): Fair enough. Tell me about the stairs at home. Are you up and down them every day?
[SEG0035] person_3 (PATIENT): Every day. It's a full flight, and the bottom few steps have no rail, because my husband was going to put one in, and then he...
[SEG0036] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He died three years ago, before he got to it. I stay over a few nights. I don't live there.
[SEG0037] person_3 (PATIENT): She stays when she's fussing. It's my own house. I'm grand in it.
[SEG0038] person_4 (DOCTOR): When the knee catches you on the way down, what eases it?
[SEG0039] person_3 (PATIENT): Sitting down. A few minutes, I don't know, and then I can carry on. The gel helps a bit, like I said.
[SEG0040] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any pain in the hip or the back, or is it the knee on its own?
[SEG0041] person_3 (PATIENT): Only the knee. The back is grand. The hip is grand.
[SEG0042] person_4 (DOCTOR): Grand. May I have a look at it?
[SEG0043] person_3 (PATIENT): These trousers are a nuisance. Hang on. There you are.

[SEG0044] person_4 (DOCTOR): Lovely. There's no redness, and it's not warm. I can't see a swelling just now. There's creaking when I bend the right knee, more than the left, and the joint feels stable.
[SEG0045] person_3 (PATIENT): There now. No swelling. I told her.
[SEG0046] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): It's not swollen this minute. Evenings are different. I'm not inventing it.

[SEG0047] person_4 (DOCTOR): It can show up later in the day, so I won't brush either of you off. My working impression is wear and tear, osteoarthritis of the right knee. That's provisional, from the stairs, the night ache, and that creaking.

[SEG0048] person_1 (NURSE): Doctor, before I slip out, I repeated the blood pressure and it's the same, one hundred and forty-eight over eighty-six. She was chatting away, so I wouldn't put it down to nerves.
[SEG0049] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The machine at home said one thirty over eighty last week. I wrote it on the calendar.
[SEG0050] person_3 (PATIENT): That yoke was my husband's. I don't know if it even works. I don't know, doctor.
[SEG0051] person_4 (DOCTOR): We'll keep both figures, ours and the one from home. Neither of them is a disaster. Niamh, you're grand to go.
[SEG0052] person_1 (NURSE): I'll be at the desk.
[SEG0053] person_4 (DOCTOR): One thing I want to come back to. You said the stomach was fine, and I only ask again because of those tablets.

[SEG0054] person_3 (PATIENT): Well, actually, I do get heartburn, I shouldn't have said no. It's a burning in the chest, mostly after the tablets, maybe twice in the week. I don't know if it's the tablets or the potatoes.
[SEG0055] person_4 (DOCTOR): I'm glad you said it. Heartburn is reason enough to leave the diclofenac tablets off. You can keep the gel, morning and night.
[SEG0056] person_3 (PATIENT): Stop them altogether? I don't know. They do take the edge off the knee.
[SEG0057] person_4 (DOCTOR): I'd still stop them. If you need something to swallow, use paracetamol, one gram, up to four times a day, with a bit of food. That's the one I'd start.
[SEG0058] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'll clear them out of the press this evening. There's a strip in the handbag too, I think.
[SEG0059] person_3 (PATIENT): Maybe. I don't know what's in the handbag. I never look.

[SEG0060] person_4 (DOCTOR): Have a glance when you're home, and don't take any more of them. On the weight, whether it's eighty-six and a half here or seventy-nine at the chemist, the knee would be happier if it came down a little. Nothing drastic.
[SEG0061] person_3 (PATIENT): I don't know if I can. The potatoes are my dinner.

[SEG0062] person_4 (DOCTOR): Smaller portions will do. For the knee itself, we could try physiotherapy, for the stairs, or a steroid injection into the joint if the night pain is the thing that's worst. I don't want to decide that today.
[SEG0063] person_3 (PATIENT): An injection? I don't know, doctor. I don't like needles. And physio is a lot of traipsing about.

[SEG0064] person_4 (DOCTOR): Then we decide nothing today. I'll see you here in six weeks anyway, and if the pain hasn't settled by then we'll choose between the physio and the injection. If the heartburn is still at you after you stop the tablets, ring us sooner, don't be waiting. Gel morning and night, no more diclofenac tablets, paracetamol if you need it, and mind that bottom step.

Keep both the clinic blood pressure and the home reading; neither figure is a disaster

spec.situation: Older patient with knee pain going down stairs and at night; uses diclofenac gel and sometimes tablets from the pharmacy; says no stomach problems and then mentions heartburn; weight discussed; physio or injection discussed, not decided.
features: relative_speaks_for_patient: a relative answers for the patient and the patient partly contradicts; reported_by follows who said it.

spoken_numbers: doses, vitals and durations are spoken as words or sloppy speech ('a hundred and two point five', 'one-forty over ninety', 'five-ish years', 'twenty milligram'); the label writes them normally (102.5, 140/90, 20 mg) and does not turn vague ones into exact ones.
disputed_numbers: the nurse reads a value and the patient or relative disagrees or remembers another (a dose, a weight, a BP). Keep both and record an uncertainty.
interruptions_trailing_off: people interrupt each other, trail off, or the answer comes two turns after the question.

omissions.text: Current diclofenac tablets are taken only sometimes, a few times a week when the stairs are bad, not daily per patient; this usage detail is missing from the medication entry.
The family member stated the diclofenac packet at home says 50 mg, supporting the nurse's reading and suggesting the dose discrepancy was partly clarified rather than entirely unresolved.

The patient denied stomach problems initially, but this was later corrected to heartburn after the tablets; the initial negative answer about stomach trouble was recorded wrongly by implication and should reflect the corrected history.
Knee pain is described as a deep ache and the knee 'catches' going down stairs; going up stairs is fine.
Turning over in bed causes the right knee to ache at night.
Rest/sitting for a few minutes eases the knee enough to carry on.
The patient denied having seen the knee swell herself.
No rail on the bottom few steps at home because the husband died before installing it; this relevant home hazard/history detail is not fully captured.
The patient is widowed; husband died three years ago.
There are no other regular medicines apart from amlodipine; vitamin D was prescribed/available but never taken and remains sealed.
Paracetamol was already available at home but the patient does not take it because she feels it does nothing for her.
Blood pressure was repeated and remained 148/86 mmHg.
The doctor advised keeping both the clinic BP and the home BP and said neither was a disaster.
The doctor told the patient not to take any more diclofenac tablets and to check the handbag at home because there may be a strip there.
Physiotherapy and steroid injection were discussed but explicitly deferred today because the patient dislikes needles and finds physio burdensome; decision postponed until review if pain not settled.
